input:
This proposal requests approval to proceed to the detailed design stage for a water recycling plant. The capital cost of the plant is $1326k, and the proposal has been appraised over a horizon of 10 years. It is important to note that the decision requested at this stage is approval of the design stage only; construction is not being requested, and no contractor has been named.

At present, the site takes its water from the mains supply and discharges its effluent to the sewer, and both of these streams flow in one direction only: water is purchased, used once, and then paid for again as it leaves the site. A recycling plant would effectively reverse part of that flow. Effluent that is currently discharged would be collected, treated, and returned to service as recycled water, and the site's purchases and discharges would both be reduced by the amount that the plant recovers. The case for the plant is essentially the case for that reversal, and the costs, the schedule, and the decision requested all follow from it.

## Case

Water enters the site as a purchased input and leaves it as a charged waste, and the site controls neither of the two prices involved. Mains water is bought at the supplier's tariff, while effluent is discharged under consent, at a cost that is set by the receiving authority and under conditions that the authority is able to tighten. A plant that recovers water from the effluent stream reduces both of these exposures at the same time: every unit of water that is recycled is a unit that does not have to be bought and a unit that does not have to be discharged.

The security of the supply represents the second ground. A site that draws the whole of its water from the mains is exposed to any interruption of that supply, whether that interruption is caused by a restriction in a dry period or by a failure in the network. A recycling plant holds part of the site's demand inside the site itself: the recovered stream continues while the store of treated water lasts, and the duties that it serves can be carried on at a reduced mains draw. The plant does not make the site independent of the mains, and the proposal does not claim that it does; it simply reduces the share of demand that an interruption would bring to a stop.

The third ground concerns the discharge itself. Effluent leaves the site under consent conditions that limit what may be discharged and in what quantity, and a consent is essentially a permission that can be reviewed. By reducing the discharged volume, the site reduces the load that the consent has to accommodate and gains headroom against a tighter consent in the future. That headroom has no line in the appraisal, and the proposal claims no money value for it; it is a ground of the case, rather than a ground of the costs.

Furthermore, the recycled water is not a substitute for mains water in every duty. It serves the duties whose quality requirements the treatment is able to meet: washdown, flushing, cooling make-up, and irrigation are the ordinary candidates on a site of this kind, while duties that involve contact with product or people remain on mains water. The plant is therefore an addition to the site's water system, not a replacement for the supply, and it is at the detailed design stage that the duties to be served are fixed and the treatment is matched to them.

## Costs

The capital cost of the plant is $1326k. This figure represents the cost of building the plant as the concept currently stands: the treatment units that clean the effluent, the storage that holds treated water against the pattern of demand, the pipework that collects the effluent and distributes the recycled water, the controls that run the plant and guard the quality of what it produces, and the installation and commissioning of the whole. It is a concept-stage figure. It is firm enough to be appraised, but it is not firm enough to build to, and converting it into a price that a contractor can actually be held to is part of what the detailed design is for.

Against the capital stand the savings that the plant is expected to make: mains water that is not bought, and effluent that is not discharged, in the quantities that the plant recovers. Between the two stand the operating costs involved in running the plant: the energy that the treatment consumes, the chemicals and media that it uses up, the maintenance of its equipment, the labour of operating it, and the monitoring that demonstrates that the recycled water meets the quality its duties require. Neither the savings nor the operating costs are stated as figures in this proposal. They are estimated in the appraisal that supports it, at the level that a concept can support, and they are the figures that the detailed design exists in order to firm up: quantities of water recovered, duty by duty, and the cost of recovering them.

The appraisal runs over a horizon of 10 years. Over the 10 years, the capital is weighed against the savings and the operating costs taken together, and no payback figure is presented as a finding of this proposal, because the figures that would carry it are concept-stage estimates. What the appraisal establishes is narrower in scope: at $1326k of capital, the scheme is worth the cost of being designed properly. The decision that commits the capital belongs to the later case, which will be built on designed quantities and tendered prices, and it is there that the saving figures will carry the weight that this proposal does not place on them.

## Schedule

Work will start one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design itself: the duties to be served are fixed, the treatment is selected against the quality that those duties require, the plant is laid out on the site, and the capital cost is rebuilt from designed quantities. Procurement follows the design, because what is to be bought cannot be specified until the design has specified it; construction follows procurement, and commissioning follows construction, ending with the plant treating effluent and supplying recycled water under its controls.

No contractor is named in this proposal. The contractor will be chosen by tender against the detailed design, and naming one at this stage would either prejudge that tender or rest the schedule on a party that has not priced the work. The schedule therefore runs from the approval, rather than from a contractor's programme: one quarter after approval the design begins, and each later stage begins when the stage before it has delivered what it needs. A construction schedule, complete with dates, belongs to the construction case and will be built from the contractor's tendered programme; this proposal commits the project to the design stage and to the sequence, and to no dates beyond the start.

## Decision requested

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design for the water recycling plant. The approval covers the design stage and nothing beyond it: it authorises the project team to fix the duties that the plant will serve, to design the treatment, storage, and distribution that the concept describes, and to rebuild the costs from designed quantities and tendered prices. It does not authorise construction, and it does not commit the capital.

The construction decision is a separate decision, which will be taken on the figures produced by the detailed design. When the design is complete, the case for construction will return with a capital cost that a contractor can be held to, savings stated duty by duty, and a schedule built from a tendered programme. If those figures do not support the plant, the project will stop at the design stage, having spent the design stage and no more. The decision that is requested now is therefore the smaller of the two decisions that the project will ask for, and it is the one that the present evidence supports: the concept is worth designing, and the design is what the remaining questions are waiting for.
